text: Cal Hacks. Hundreds of people in one hangar, and any one of them could change what you build.
Meeting people in person is still how teams and ideas start.
But while you talk to one person, you can't talk to anyone else.
So every hello is a gamble. In one study, ninety five percent of guests wanted to meet new people, yet half their conversations were with friends they already knew.
What if the room had a filter?
Meet the Human Human Interaction Lab. Your phone, on a lanyard, becomes a live name badge.
You onboard by text. Our iMessage agent asks who you are and who you want to meet, and sends you its contact card.
Your badge shows your name, huge, and the topics people should ask you about.
Behind the scenes, every pair of attendees is scored in both directions. Only mutual matches light up.
Wear the badge and walk the room. As a match comes closer, measured by Ultra Wideband, both badges tint toward a shared color, and the topics flip to what they want to talk to you about.
Within two meters, the avatars jump together, and the conversation starts recording, with consent.
When you part ways, you get a summary and a follow up you can send.
And everyone you met lives in your People list.
Under the hood, the iPhone ranges nearby badges and syncs live to Convex, with SpacetimeDB as a second backend. Photon carries the conversation over iMessage.
TypeSafe's Jev rates every pair in half a second, Claude writes why you should meet, and a geometric mean makes one sided interest score low.
Every screen, avatar and sound was designed in Figma first.
Human Human Interaction Lab. Fewer gambles, better hellos.
